info.text: Formative Knowledge Check Quiz for Module_02_Cataloguing: Module 02 Knowledge Check Quiz.

name.text: 01 Question: Authority Files vs. Local Shelfmarks

questiontext.text: Why are global authority identifiers (such as Trismegistos numbers or Pinakes records) essential in digital manuscript cataloguing rather than relying solely on local library shelfmarks?

generalfeedback.text: Global authority IDs (e.g. Trismegistos, Pinakes) provide persistent, language-independent identification across dispersed collections.

answer.text: Because local shelfmarks can change during institutional reorganizations or vary in spelling across languages, whereas authority URIs provide persistent, unambiguous identifiers across international databases.

feedback.text: Correct. Authority files disambiguate manuscripts whose library names, cities, or catalogue call numbers vary across centuries and publications.

answer.text: Because local shelfmarks are copyright-protected by holding libraries and cannot be published online.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Shelfmarks are historical catalogue numbers and are not copyright-restricted.

answer.text: Because Trismegistos stores the full high-resolution photographic scans of every manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Trismegistos is a metadata authority database, not an image repository.

answer.text: Because authority identifiers automatically translate Greek manuscripts into English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Authority records track cataloguing identifiers and textual metadata, not linguistic translation.

name.text: 02 Question: Canonical Text Services (CTS) URN Syntax

questiontext.text: In the Canonical Text Services (CTS) URN architecture, what structural hierarchy is encoded in the identifier urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc1:1.1?

generalfeedback.text: CTS URNs encode a rigorous conceptual hierarchy: namespace -> textgroup -> work -> edition -> passage citation.

answer.text: Namespace, textgroup (Homer), work (Iliad), version/edition, and specific passage citation (Book 1, Line 1).

feedback.text: Correct. CTS URNs express a strict conceptual hierarchy moving from author/textgroup down to specific passage citations.

answer.text: The physical GPS coordinates of the library where the manuscript is housed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTS URNs cite abstract textual works and passages, not physical buildings.

answer.text: The IP address and TCP port number of the Moodle web server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTS URNs are uniform resource names for philological citation, not network addresses.

answer.text: The date and timestamp of the most recent Git commit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTS URNs follow Homer Multitext citation ontology, independent of version control timestamps.

questiontext.text: Under the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI P5) guidelines, which element is the mandatory container for all codicological, palaeographical, and administrative metadata describing a manuscript witness?

generalfeedback.text: within is the canonical TEI container for structured manuscript cataloguing and codicological data.

answer.text: <msDesc> (Manuscript Description) within the <sourceDesc> of the <teiHeader>.

feedback.text: Correct. The element holds the structured codicological hierarchy, including identification, contents, physical description, and history.

answer.text: <body> inside <text>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The element contains the primary transcription text, not the codicological metadata.

answer.text: <encodingDesc> inside <profileDesc>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. documents the editorial and transcription principles applied during encoding.

answer.text: <revisionDesc> inside <front>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. documents the change log of the XML file itself.

name.text: 04 Question: Physical Description Hierarchy in TEI

questiontext.text: Which TEI element specifically structures information about the material support, quire collation, foliation, and page layout of a codex?

generalfeedback.text: houses the physical architecture of the codex: support, collation, dimensions, script, and binding.

answer.text: <physDesc> (Physical Description), containing children such as <objectDesc>, <supportDesc>, and <layoutDesc>.

feedback.text: Correct. is the specialized sub-tree in dedicated to material aspects of the manuscript artifact.

answer.text: <msContents>, which lists the modern scholars who purchased the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. lists the intellectual works, titles, and rubrics contained within the manuscript.

answer.text: <history>, which records the grammar rules of ancient Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. records provenance, acquisition, and former owners.

answer.text: <additional>, which stores student quiz grades.

feedback.text: Incorrect. holds administrative notes and surrogate image details.

questiontext.text: In classical codicology, what does the collation formula 1–5⁸, 6⁶ (fol. 46) indicate about the physical construction of a manuscript?

generalfeedback.text: Collation formulae represent the quire structure (gatherings) and leaf counts that constitute the codicological body.

answer.text: The codex consists of five quires of 8 leaves (quaterniones) followed by one quire of 6 leaves (ternio), totaling 46 leaves.

feedback.text: Correct. Standard collation notation records quire indices with superscript leaf counts and total foliation.

answer.text: The manuscript was written by five different scribes over six centuries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The numbers represent quires (gatherings) and leaves, not scribal personnel.

answer.text: The text has five chapters of 8 verses each and six footnotes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation formulae describe the physical gatherings of parchment/paper, not text divisions.

answer.text: The codex was sold five times for eight gold florins.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation formulae are structural binding formulas.

name.text: 06 Question: Dublin Core vs. TEI msDesc

questiontext.text: Why is standard Dublin Core (DC) metadata insufficient on its own for critical manuscript scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: TEI msDesc provides the hierarchical depth required for physical codicology that flat standards like Dublin Core cannot represent.

answer.text: Dublin Core uses flat, 15-property key-value pairs designed for modern bibliographies, whereas TEI msDesc models deeply nested, composite codicological realities like multiple scribal hands, palimpsests, and quire repairs.

feedback.text: Correct. Dublin Core is too flat and generic to capture the intricate multi-tiered physical and historical nuances of premodern manuscripts.

answer.text: Dublin Core is an obsolete proprietary format that cannot be viewed on modern computers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dublin Core is an active, universal metadata standard (ISO 15836), but it lacks domain depth for codicology.

answer.text: Dublin Core is illegal under European open-access copyright legislation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dublin Core is completely open and public-domain.

answer.text: Dublin Core does not permit dates earlier than 1900 CE.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dublin Core allows historical dates, but lacks structural fields for material codicology.

name.text: 07 Question: Linked Open Data and URIs

questiontext.text: How does expressing manuscript metadata as RDF triples (Subject–Predicate–Object) with dereferenceable URIs improve scholarly discovery?

generalfeedback.text: RDF triples and linked data URIs connect isolated manuscript records into a global, queryable scholarly knowledge graph.

answer.text: It allows disparate library catalogues across the world to be queried as a single decentralized graph database, automatically connecting manuscripts with linked bibliographies, gazetteers, and prosopographies.

feedback.text: Correct. RDF linked data enables automated federated SPARQL queries across international institutional silos.

answer.text: It encrypts library records to prevent unauthorized public access.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linked Open Data is designed for open, frictionless interoperability.

answer.text: It converts all ancient manuscripts into modern MP3 audiobooks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RDF is a knowledge graph data model, not an audio conversion format.

answer.text: It replaces all human librarians with automated cataloguing bots.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linked data assists scholars and librarians by interconnecting semantic metadata.

name.text: 08 Question: LLM Hallucinations in Codicological Extraction

questiontext.text: When using Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically convert unstructured 19th-century Latin catalogue descriptions into TEI XML, what is a common hallucination risk?

generalfeedback.text: LLMs can hallucinate plausible-sounding codicological details; automated schema validation and manual verification are mandatory.

answer.text: The LLM may fabricate plausible-sounding folio counts, invent watermarks, or confabulate shelfmarks that appear syntactically valid but do not exist in the source document.

feedback.text: Correct. Probabilistic language models optimize for plausible fluent text and can invent specific historical numbers or codicological details.

answer.text: The LLM will refuse to process any text written in Latin or Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern LLMs handle Latin and ancient Greek fluently.

answer.text: The LLM will alter the physical parchment in the library vault.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software models interact only with digital representations, not physical artifacts.

answer.text: The LLM will automatically delete the Git repository if an error is encountered.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLM inference does not execute destructive repository commands unless piped into unmonitored scripts.

questiontext.text: Why is ISO Schematron used alongside RelaxNG or XML Schema in professional TEI metadata pipelines?

generalfeedback.text: Schematron enforces contextual business rules and philological constraints that structural schemas cannot express.

answer.text: Schematron can validate complex co-occurrence constraints and business logic (e.g. asserting that if a manuscript is marked 'fragment', foliation must be under 5 leaves) that grammar-based schemas cannot express.

feedback.text: Correct. Schematron uses XPath expressions to test rule-based contextual dependencies and logical constraints across XML documents.

answer.text: Schematron is the only tool that can translate Greek into Latin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron is a structural and semantic XML validation language.

answer.text: Schematron is required to compile Python scripts into executable machine code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron is an XML validation standard, not a Python compiler.

answer.text: Schematron automatically writes student research papers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron is an automated validation engine.

name.text: 10 Question: The Role of Controlled Vocabularies

questiontext.text: Why should TEI metadata attributes (such as @script, @material, or @ruling) use values drawn from controlled vocabularies (e.g. Getty AAT or CERL thesauri)?

generalfeedback.text: Controlled vocabularies guarantee semantic consistency across independent cataloguing projects and search engines.

answer.text: Controlled vocabularies eliminate synonymous variations (e.g. 'parchment' vs. 'vellum' vs. 'pergamentum'), enabling precise computational filtering and cross-corpus aggregation.

feedback.text: Correct. Standardized ontologies ensure that identical concepts are indexed consistently regardless of local linguistic preference.

answer.text: Because using uncontrolled strings results in immediate criminal copyright prosecution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Controlled vocabularies are a scholarly best practice for interoperability, not a criminal matter.

answer.text: Because controlled vocabularies reduce the size of the XML file by 95%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Vocabulary control improves semantic consistency, not file compression.

answer.text: Because controlled vocabularies make text unreadable to humans.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Controlled terms use clear natural language concepts mapped to persistent URIs.
